en: General Discussion of the Heart Sutra, Revised by the Disciple You Wanjun. The Heart Sutra says:
Form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is not different from form. Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form. (Zhu)
Sheng asked, "What do you mean by this? Linzi replied, "If you can know the place where form and emptiness do not reach, then these four phrases will become clear to you of their own accord.
Sheng asked again about the place where form and emptiness do not reach. Linzi said, "The place where form and emptiness do not reach is your true mind;
it is your actual ground. Now, since it is called 'the place where form and emptiness do not reach,' and yet—"
Furthermore, it is said: "The true mind and the ground of reality—how could there be a place where form and emptiness do not reach that still possesses the true mind as the ground of reality?
Master Linzi said: "Form is form. Once one has attained it as form, one can likewise attain it as emptiness.
Emptiness is emptiness. Once one has attained it as emptiness, one can likewise attain it as form. This is the dust.
The arising of dust and its cessation are matters of relative opposition; they likely do not constitute your true mind or actual ground.
Yet, in your true mind and actual ground, there is fundamentally no form—so who could empty it? There is fundamentally no emptiness—so who could form it?
Regarding the sutras on form and emptiness, I have once imitated their phrasing and adopted them, saying: "Arising is not different [from emptiness]."
Cessation is not different from arising; arising is itself cessation, and cessation is itself arising. Yet, how could one color this true mind and true ground?
If there is no form, there is no cessation. Furthermore, how could one empty it? If there is no emptiness, there is no arising.
When both form and emptiness are utterly empty, and both arising and cessation are utterly extinguished—this is the point where form, emptiness, arising, and cessation do not reach.
This is the locus. A Buddhist scripture says: "When arising and ceasing have ceased, tranquil extinction is bliss.
I have also once imitated its phrasing and adopted it, saying: "When form is empty and emptiness has ceased, true emptiness is bliss.

Viewed from this perspective, the emptiness of "form-emptiness" is merely the cessation of the arising and ceasing of dust-like phenomena. Yet, why is it called "true emptiness"? Master Lin said: "Non-arising."
It is neither extinguished; it is neither defiled nor pure; it neither increases nor decreases. This is why it is "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).

Yet, from the beginning there is no form (*rūpa*), and from the beginning there is no sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*). All things are already fully manifest; what need, then, is there to rely upon emptiness to empty them?
Therefore, that which is called the "True Mind" (*bhūtamanas*) is the true nature inherently possessed by me—the sovereign Bodhisattva. Truly...
The Earth is the realm where I possess nothing; it is the immovable site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Herein I have come to know that the true mind and the real ground are the gate of non-duality. The true mind and the real ground are the stage of *samādhi*.
The true mind and the real ground are the place of non-arising. The true mind and the real ground are the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. There is none...
There is grasping but no relinquishing; there is no dependence and no leaning. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"If one grasps at the marks of dharmas, one clings to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. If one grasps at the marks of non-dharmas, one likewise clings to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.

In the past, there was an interpreter who said: "The marks of dharmas pertain to existence (*sat*), while the marks of non-dharmas pertain to non-existence (*asat*). Is what is called 'existence' not simply form (*rūpa*)?"
That which is called "non-existence"—is this not emptiness? To have form and yet have emptiness is to have grasping and abandoning;

to have grasping and abandoning is to have dependence and reliance. As for that which is the true mind and reality itself—the realm where form and emptiness do not reach—is there the characteristic of existence therein?
Is there the characteristic of non-existence therein? Is there the notion of self, person, sentient being, or life-span therein?
Is it one who has taking and rejecting, or dependence and reliance?
Yet, as for the true mind and the actual ground, they cannot be manifested through words—thus Confucius spoke of them but rarely;
they cannot be known by hearing—thus Zigong was unable to hear of them; they cannot be attained through talent—thus Yanzi desired to follow him but could not.

Indeed. Formerly, the Great Master Datong of the Tang dynasty, because he did not clarify the teaching of the ultimate principle, taught people that they could see their nature and become Buddhas, saying, "Your original nature is like empty space. Yet the Sixth Patriarch criticized this, saying it was still "possessing cognition and views.
Is the true mind and the actual ground something that belongs to cognition and views? Or does it not belong to cognition [and views]?

It is so. I have often observed these two characters, "knowledge" (zhi) and "vision" (jian), and thereby understood that the knowledge and vision of Great Penetration is precisely the emptiness of form and emptiness;
it is the empty space of the mutual opposition between form and emptiness, wherein dust arises and dust perishes.
It is not the emptiness within space, but rather the emptiness that is neither born nor extinguished—the void where the emptiness of form does not reach.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Do not grasp at marks; suchness is immovable. Form has the mark of form, and emptiness has the mark of emptiness, yet suchness remains immovable.
This is the true mind and the actual ground of my own being, the manifestation of all things. True.
The true ground of the mind—how could it fall into the two marks of the arising and ceasing of dust-like phenomena, such as form and emptiness?
If one knows this handle and reaches this stage, it is simply a matter of wearing clothes and eating food; what else remains?
Those who have personally reached the other shore should know this for themselves.
Master Hong asked about the meaning of the word "much" (or "vast"). Master Lin said:
"That which I call the 'true ground of the other shore,' where neither form nor emptiness reaches, is that which possesses great wisdom—it is my own true mind.
And this true mind of mine pervades the true ground of the other shore, being as vast as this; it encompasses all things."
It is manifest. Therefore, the true ground of the other shore has no boundaries; it is neither square nor round, neither large nor small;
it is neither blue, yellow, nor white; it is neither above nor below, neither long nor short; it is without anger and without joy, without right and without wrong, without good and without evil;
it has neither beginning nor end—it all exists within the true ground of my own other shore. And that true ground of the other shore...
The extent of the earth is fundamentally such that it is vast; all things are fully manifested therein—whether born from a womb, born from an egg, born from moisture, or born by transformation;
whether possessing form or being formless; whether possessing perception or being without perception.
If one is neither with perception nor without perception, one dwells entirely within the ground of reality on my other shore.
As for the extent of that ground of reality on the other shore, it is inherently so vast that all things are spontaneously perfected: the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
From where have they come? Can the empty space of the eastern direction ever be measured or conceptualized?
Can the empty space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir ever be measured or conceptualized?
Yet that shore, the ground of reality, exhausts the infinite emptiness of the four cardinal directions—east, south, west, and north—and the four intermediate directions, as well as above and below;
it is itself empty. And how could this infinite emptiness possibly be measured or conceived? Looking upward, one does not see heaven;
looking downward, one does not see earth. Therefore it is said: throughout the worlds of the ten directions, this is precisely [it].
The body of the Dharma King: the entirety of the worlds throughout the ten directions is this very gate of liberation;

the entirety of the worlds throughout the ten directions is a single volume of the Tathāgata’s sutra. Viewed from this perspective, how could the entirety of the worlds throughout the ten directions not reside within my own ground of the other shore?
And within that ground of the other shore, can there be the mark of a self, or the mark of a person?
Is there a mark of a sentient being? Is there a mark of a life-span? Within the reality-ground of the other shore (*pāra*), there are fundamentally no self, person, sentient being, or life-span;
everything is primordially perfected. Therefore, those who take refuge in the Buddha take refuge in the awakening within this reality-ground of the other shore.
Those who take refuge in the Dharma take refuge in this reality-ground of the other shore.
This is what is meant by correctness. To take refuge in the Saṅgha is to take refuge in that which is purified within the reality-ground of this shore and the other shore.
If one abandons the reality-ground to seek a "true mind," or if one leaves the other shore to seek Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one has strayed far indeed.
Now, that which is called the true mind is the self-nature (*svabhāva*). And the actual ground of the true mind is the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*).
Therefore it is said: "The ground of the mind is nothing other than the precept of self-nature; the ground of the mind being free from delusion is the wisdom of self-nature;

the ground of the mind being free from distraction is the concentration of self-nature. When the true mind is its actual ground, everything is fully realized. All Buddhas of the three periods of time have emerged from within this.
The unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment all emerges from within this. Now, the reality of the far shore is a sublime meaning;
it is thus unsurpassed and profoundly deep. Those who have personally reached the far shore shall know it for themselves.
Master Chen asked, "Regarding what you have said—that the five aggregates are all empty—is this the emptiness of form, or is it the emptiness within emptiness?
Master Lin replied, "This so-called emptiness is the emptiness within emptiness; it is without dharmas and without marks.
It does not depend upon anything to be empty; rather, it is the fundamental substance in which all things are spontaneously perfected."

This is the natural state [of things]. Furthermore, fearing that they might not yet clearly understand the principle that illumination has nothing upon which it illuminates, and thus negate phenomena through the concept of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) while falling into the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*), the text subsequently addresses Śāriputra twice and warns him with such words as "form is no different from emptiness.
It further states: "Are these marks of the emptiness of all phenomena not themselves the marks of form? Emptiness...
Is it not a matter of characteristics? Now, the characteristic of form is certainly not empty;

yet, when one empties it by means of the emptiness of all dharmas, this remains inseparable from dharmas and inseparable from characteristics. To empty something by depending upon emptiness—how can this be called a "ready-made koan," the spontaneity of the fundamental essence?
The *Platform Sutra* says: "Good friends, do not hear my teaching of emptiness and then immediately become attached to emptiness. First of all, do not be attached to emptiness.

If you sit in meditation with an empty mind, you will become attached to a state of indeterminate emptiness. It further says: "Moreover, there are deluded people who sit in meditation with an empty mind..."
Having no thoughts at all, they claim for themselves to be "Great. Such people as these cannot be spoken with, because of their false views.
This so-called emptiness is merely the emptiness of empty characteristics; how could it be called the emptiness within emptiness?
The Three Chapters of the Daotong Jing (Scripture of the Great Pervasion of the Dao). The first, the Chapter on True Emptiness, says: "It is born before Heaven;
though born, it has no form. It exists after Heaven; though existing, it has no substance. Yet, that which has no substance has never ceased to exist.
Therefore, it is called 'inconceivable. Now, if one speaks of 'no form,' can there still be birth? And if one speaks of 'no substance,' can there still be existence?"
Ah! It arises from non-arising; it arises while there is nothing that arises. It exists in non-existence; it exists while there is nothing that exists. It takes form in formlessness;
it takes form while there is nothing that takes form. It embodies itself in non-embodiment; it embodies itself while there is nothing to embody.
To know this is to understand the wondrous meaning of true emptiness; it is truly impossible to conjecture or conceive through discursive thought.
In its second chapter, "The Profound Principle," it says: "Like space, it is without marks, serene and perfectly complete.

In its third chapter, "The Profound Mystery," it says: "Suchness is spontaneous; vast and without boundary. Judging from this, it is clear that what it calls the "mark of emptiness" is not the true emptiness within emptiness.
Where there is a mark, there is seeing; where there is seeing, there is attachment. How could this not fall [into the trap of conceptualization]?

At the ultimate limit, it is called the profound stillness, the perfect fulfillment, the suchness of spontaneity. Therefore, if one wishes to recognize true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there is no emptiness that can be recognized.
Since there is nothing to be recognized, how can one recognize "this is emptiness"? Is this emptiness not emptiness? Or is non-emptiness emptiness?
Whether one says it is empty or says it is not empty, both involve the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) and are not called true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*).

True emptiness is without the mark of emptiness; where there is no mark of emptiness, that is true emptiness. Yet this is also found in the Way (*Dào*). It is said: "Emptiness without emptiness, yet having emptiness.

It is also said: "Not empty within emptiness, yet being empty. It is also said: "Emptiness has no fixed emptiness. It is also said: "Knowing emptiness is non-emptiness. It is also said: "Recognizing the dharma of non-emptiness. And so forth.
He said, "Not clinging to the view of emptiness—this is the true emptiness within all emptiness; it is the wondrous meaning of true emptiness.

Suseng asked, "Why is it called 'emptiness within'? Master Linzi replied, "Have you not heard of what is called the 'Centrality' (*zhong*) of the *Zhongyong*, where joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused?
This Centrality before arousal is precisely 'emptiness within. It is spontaneously present."
This is what is called the "public case" (gong'an): it is that which is neither form nor emptiness.

Precisely because it is neither form nor emptiness, it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, and neither increasing nor decreasing. That which constitutes the fundamental substance of the ground of reality is the "central state prior to manifestation" (the unmanifested Mean).
The *Zhongyong* says: "How could there be anything upon which to rely? This does not merely mean that one is empty of form and does not rely on the forms produced by the mundane;
it also means that one is empty of emptiness itself and does not rely on the emptiness resulting from the cessation of the mundane.
If one were to say, "I am empty," and lean slightly toward that emptiness, this would constitute being attached to the emptiness of the mundane's cessation.
Yet it is not empty. Master Lin said:
"The state of 'the mean' when joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused is what I call the place where form and emptiness do not reach;
it is my fundamental substance, my great void. When I bring myself to abide in this mean, I restore [it to its original state]."
The fundamental substance of the self is the Great Void of the self. Since the fundamental substance of the self is the Great Void and is central, harmony arises spontaneously.
Once harmony has arisen, how could heaven and earth not find their proper places? How could the myriad things not be nurtured?
That they are situated and nurtured—all issues forth from this; everything is already perfected. How could there be anything upon which it relies?
And who is it that acts for them?
Mr. Lin asked: "Is not the 'central state before arousal' what the *Shijing* refers to as 'without sound and without smell'? Master Lin said:
"Indeed. However, the emptiness of the place where form and emptiness do not reach is certainly described as being without sound and without smell, yet it is not [mere] nothingness."
It is dusty. Yet, as for the emptiness that exists in opposition to form, how could it possess sound, odor, or dust?

Master Lin said: "Although the emptiness of form-and-emptiness is said to be free from the dust of sound and odor, if one raises the sound within that emptiness of form-and-emptiness, then even the emptiness of form-and-emptiness can be rendered dusty by that sound."
Set its stench within the emptiness of form-emptiness, and even that emptiness of form-emptiness may be defiled by the stench.
But as for that which is beyond the reach of the emptiness of celestial space—can it be sounded?
Can it be stunk? Can it be defiled? This is precisely the realm of sound and stench... [is it not?]
Where the dust of the mundane world does not reach, all things are spontaneously perfected. Those who have personally reached the other shore should know this for themselves.
The *Zhongyong* says: "Majestic is its benevolence; profound is its depth; vast is its heaven. All of these are my own true mind.
It is the true ground where all things are manifested and perfected. Herein the great constants of the world are woven;
herein the great root of the world is established. Herein the transformative and nurturing processes of Heaven and Earth are known.
All beings possessing vital breath revere and love it here. And herein lies my own nature.
The nature of humanity, the nature of things, and the nature of Heaven and Earth—all are fully realized, harmonized, and assisted herein.
This is why Heaven and Earth are so great, and why King Wen is called "Wen" (the Cultivated).
As for those who personally reach the other shore, they should know it for themselves.
Zheng asked, "What is called the true mind? What is called the ground of reality? Linzi said, "The state of 'centrality before arousal' is the ground of reality of the true mind;
however, once it is aroused and accords with the measure, it is no longer called the ground of reality."
Is this not the true mind? That which is quiescent and unmoving is the actual ground of the true mind;
yet that which responds and thereby penetrates everything—is this not called the true mind as the actual ground?
Master Linzi said: "The true ground of the true mind is one *Houtu* diagram; it is fundamentally beyond description in terms of sound or smell.
The true mind as the true ground is one *Luoshu* diagram; therein, its initial manifestations can be perceived."
Linzi said: "That which can be turned from form into emptiness is emptiness amidst the dust;
that which can be turned from emptiness into form is form amidst the dust. It is like a vessel: originally empty, it becomes form when filled;
it is the form of what was filled, yet when its contents are removed, it is once again empty. This is why emptiness has coming and going—it is the arising of the dust."
This refers to its cessation, rather than its original non-existence.
Master Lin said: "To know that form is empty and to take that as emptiness certainly cannot be considered true emptiness;
yet to know the emptiness of emptiness and to take that as emptiness likewise cannot be considered true emptiness. To know the emptiness of...
To take that which is empty as being "emptiness" is certainly not yet to have attained emptiness;
likewise, to take that which is the point where the emptiness of form reaches its limit as being "emptiness" is also not yet to have attained emptiness. Master Lin asked:
"Now, if one takes that which is the point where the emptiness of form reaches its limit as being 'emptiness,' is it truly not yet to have attained emptiness? Master Lin—
The disciple said, "Since there is still someone present who possesses knowledge, how much more so could one say that one considers oneself empty?
Linzi said, "Regarding that which is beyond the reach of both form and emptiness, yet is called 'dwelling'—does it have a location?
Or does it have no location? Does it reside within my own body? Does it reside outside my own body? Does it reside in heaven?"
Is it within the earth? Or is it beyond the heavens and the earth? Can it be made ancient? Can it be made contemporary?
Is it impossible to make it ancient? Is it impossible to make it contemporary? To speak in essence:
where is there that is not my own true ground? Where is there that is not the true ground of non-self?
Where is there that is not my true mind? Where is there that is not the true mind that is non-self?
Only those who have personally reached the other shore shall know this for themselves.
Linzi said: "As for that place where neither form nor emptiness reaches—is there a sovereign bodhisattva there? Can one perceive it?
There is no sovereign bodhisattva, and there is no non-sovereign bodhisattva. There is no perception, and there is no non-perception."
"Is there a 'far shore'? Can one attain and reach it? There is no far shore, nor is there the absence of a far shore. There is no reaching, nor is there the absence of reaching.
Master Linzi said: "The entire *Heart Sūtra* is intended to lead one toward the Supreme Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Therefore, as for 'contemplation' (*pratyavekṣaṇā*):"
Regarding this contemplation (*vipaśyanā*): although contemplation possesses a method, it is devoid of intentional action. For where there is intentional action, there are signs (*nimitta*);
where there are signs, there is attachment (*saṅga*). If there are signs and attachment, one lacks sovereignty; how, then, could such a person be called the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara?
The Fourth Patriarch, Daoxin, at the age of fourteen, came to pay his respects to the Third Patriarch, Sengcan, saying, "I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will grant me liberation.
The Third Patriarch asked, "Who has bound you? He replied, "No one has bound me. The Third Patriarch said, "Why then do you seek liberation?
Is this not what is called the 'spontaneous perfection' of all things for a sovereign Bodhisattva? And so he personally arrived there.
"Regarding 'the shore,' you should know it for yourself.
Linzi asked, "In the ultimate teaching of the Śākya, why is it called both the 'Gate of Nature' and the 'Gate of Emptiness'?"
That which is fundamentally empty by nature is true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Therefore, persons and dharmas are defilements (*rajas*), and one empties these defilements.
That which performs the emptying is itself a defilement. Knowledge and views (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*) are defilements, and one empties these defilements;

that which performs the emptying is itself a defilement. To give rise to the mind is called delusion (*moha*); delusion is a defilement. To empty the mind is likewise a defilement of the deluded mind. This is the domain of the mental faculty (*manas*).
What was previously called "desire" refers to the dust of the sensory realm. To intend toward something while remaining empty of it is likewise a dust toward which one is directed;
how could this be called the teaching of the ultimate limit, or the true emptiness of the gate of nature?
The Sūtra says: "These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness. Master Linzi said: "Form (rūpa) is an object; it is certainly not empty in itself.
Yet, by means of the dharma of emptiness, one empties that form—this is the 'characteristic of emptiness' of all dharmas. The object is there, but it is not [inherently] empty.
Feeling (vedanā) is an object; it is certainly not empty in itself. Yet, by means of the dharma of emptiness, one empties that feeling—this is..."
This is the mark of emptiness of all phenomena; it is the dust, yet it is not emptiness itself. It is likewise with perception, mental formations, and consciousness. A Buddhist scripture states:
"Among all things, do not give rise to the notion of signlessness. If one were to take the emptiness that results from the cessation of various forms as [the ultimate], [it would be a delusion].
Emptiness gives rise to signlessness. Once signlessness has arisen, it is itself a sign. Therefore, the mind that gives rise to signs is a defilement;
the mind that gives rise to signlessness is likewise a defilement.

The *Samādhi Sūtra* states: "When the mind is devoid of the characteristics of mind, it does not grasp at the characteristic of empty space, does not rely upon the various stages (*bhūmi*), and does not abide in wisdom;

this is the *prajñāpāramitā*. If one does not yet know that the mind is fundamentally without characteristics, yet grasps at the characteristic of empty space to treat things as empty, how can this be called the great wisdom that reaches the other shore? The Śākya [Buddha] also spoke thus.
It is said: "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" refers to true nature (*dharmatā*). It is further said: "All wriggling and sentient beings share one and the same nature.
Thus, among all myriad things, there is not one that does not manifest its form and characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
Is this not the fact that the true ground is omnipresent, the true mind is all-encompassing, and everything is spontaneously perfected? And yet—
"Those who have personally reached the other shore should know this for themselves.
Huang Sheng said, "Does the true ground of the real mind have a fixed location, or does it not?
Linzi said, "How could it be that it has a fixed location? How could it be that it does not have a fixed location? Where is it not present?"
The Great Void—where is there that is not my true ground? Where is there that is not my true ground? Where is there that is not my true mind?
When the true mind is once raised, it possesses great *dhāraṇī*. Is this not like pulling the main rope of a net;
would its meshes then not open wide? Therefore, my true ground may be likened to a net. It can be so.
It encompasses heaven and earth and all things so completely that there is nothing beyond it. My true mind is like the main rope of a net;
by means of it, one can sustain the vastness of heaven, earth, and all things without fail. If this is so, then is the true mind and the reality-ground not indeed as great as this?
The *Zhongyong* says: "When one attains the ultimate harmony of the Mean and the Correct, heaven and earth find their proper places, and all things flourish."
All things are nurtured therein. As for the true mind and the reality-ground, they are indeed as vast as this;
they are the spontaneous perfection of all things. Only those who have personally reached the other shore shall know this for themselves.

Huang Sheng said, "I have now heard your instructions regarding the principle of the Great Total Retention (Mahādhāraṇī). May I venture to ask why it is called 'complete'? Master Lin said, "'Complete' means..."
It is complete within it. Yet, this completeness surely resides within me. However, is there something upon which it is complete? Or is there nothing upon which it is complete?
Is it complete in some things but incomplete in others? Or is it complete in nothing yet complete in everything?
Is it complete within the true mind and the ground of reality, as a great total retention (*mahā-dhāraṇī*)? Or is it not complete within the true...?
Is it not the true ground of the mind and the Great Dhāraṇī? If so, is the true mind and the true ground not indeed as wondrous as this?
The *Zhongyong* says: "For one who acts thus, there is manifestation without being seen, transformation without movement, and accomplishment without action."
Thus, it is likewise as divine; all things are spontaneously accomplished. Those who have personally reached the other shore should know this for themselves.
The *I Ching* says: "Change and movement do not abide; they circulate through the six voids. Now, what are called the "six voids" are not what I mean by them.
Is it truly a solid ground? However, it is clear that the six voids are not solid ground. Why, then, is it called "solid ground"?
It is because the absence of solid ground is itself solid ground; whereas the presence of solid ground means it is not solid ground.
Is it not the case that whatever possesses form and appearance must eventually perish? Since there is a time of destruction, how can it be called "solid ground"?
A Daoist scripture says: "Only when empty space is pulverized does one's entire body reveal itself. Now, as for "empty space," it is merely empty space.
Yet, when it is said that "empty space is pulverized," can empty space actually be pulverized?
The reason it is said that empty space is pulverized is likely because it does not take the emptiness of "form-emptiness" (*rūpa-śūnyatā*) to be true emptiness. Master Zeng said: "Form-emptiness..."
"Regarding this emptiness: it is empty. Yet, is the emptiness of that place where the emptiness of form does not reach not also empty? Linzi said:
"The emptiness of the emptiness of form possesses that emptiness; however, the emptiness of the place where the emptiness of form does not reach possesses no such emptiness.
Since there is no emptiness yet nothing that is not empty, it is said that both existence and non-existence are not established, and there is no 'having'."
Furthermore, how can there be "existence" when there is no "non-existence"? How can there be "emptiness"?
The Buddhist teachings state: "One should employ great wisdom to shatter the five aggregates, afflictions, and worldly toil.
It also says: "To shatter empty space with a single fist. Now, since one possesses great wisdom and has reached the other shore (*pāramitā*), how could there be [any such things]?

This is to be attached to the false view that there is empty space. To claim that this very non-attachment to empty space constitutes "breaking through empty space" is already to break through empty space itself;
how much more so for the five aggregates, afflictions, and worldly toil?

This is because it is said that within the true ground of the other shore, there is fundamentally no empty space, and there are fundamentally no five aggregates, afflictions, or worldly toil. Now, since...
"You have reached the other shore. Where, then, are those things formerly called the five aggregates, afflictions, and worldly toil, as well as the false views of emptiness?
Therefore, it is said: 'Shatter them! Qiu asked for the meaning of 'shattering,' and Master Lin replied:"
The meaning of "breaking through" (daiha) refers to non-existence (*abhāva*).
If it were merely a matter of words, could one then speak of "breaking through" the so-called five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and worldly toil (*saṃsāra*)?

Yet, while the five aggregates, afflictions, and worldly toil can still be described, could one then speak of "breaking through" what is called "empty space" (*ākāśa*)? And yet, you say, "break through the five aggregates."
Those who possess afflictions, worldly toil, emptiness, and false views are merely returning to my original non-being;
as for those who personally reach the other shore, they shall know this for themselves.
Daochuan said: "Where form and sound do not create obstruction, one personally arrives at the City of the Dharma King. Now, what is meant by "personally arriving at the City of the Dharma King"?
Is this not called "reaching the other shore"? Yet, within that other shore, there are fundamentally no eyes or ears. Since there are no eyes or ears...
An said, "There is neither form nor sound.
Śākyamuni replied, "Sin and merit have no master; yet the true ground of the other shore is precisely a place where sin and merit do not reach."
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "There is a great *dhāraṇī* gate called Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*), from which flow forth all true suchness (*tathatā*) and nirvāṇa.
Is this so-called "great *dhāraṇī* gate" not what I call the "ground of reality"?
Is this so-called "true suchness and nirvāṇa" not what I call the "true mind"?
Linzi said: "I have once heard the bequeathed teachings of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: 'Where there is form, there is seeing; when form ceases, there is no seeing.

Where there is sound, there is hearing; when sound vanishes, there is no hearing. If one were to take the cessation of form and the absence of seeing as emptiness, how would that differ from taking the vanishing of sound and the absence of hearing as emptiness? Now, as for form and sound..."
All are dust. As dust, they appear as form and sound; as dust, they perish and become emptiness.
Within this reality of the other shore, what is there to see? What is there to hear? There exists only the true nature of seeing and hearing.
If one does not know that seeing and hearing possess this true nature, yet claims, "I can remain without acting," such a person is deluded.
One is driven by the dust of forms and sounds; thus, one might cover the eyes to avoid forms and block the ears to escape sounds.
Yet, it seems that the Buddha’s Dharma is not like this.
Mr. Pan asked, "The Master says that 'true mind' and 'actual ground' are places where there is no birth. Yet you also say they are the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods. Why is this?
Master Lin said, "A mother takes the act of giving birth as her defining characteristic, yet for birth itself, non-birth is what constitutes its greatness.
An ancient said, 'All dharmas are without birth. Now, since all dharmas are without birth,"
If so, then by what means could it be considered the mother of the Buddhas of the three periods? Nevertheless, within the true mind and the reality-ground, all dharmas are fully present;
this is that from which the Buddhas of the three periods arise. And as for the manner in which they arise:
When that which arises from the true mind and the ground of reality arises as something arisen, it cannot be known.
When that which arises from the true mind and the ground of reality arises as nothing arisen, it cannot be known. Truly, the real is unspeakable;
it is unspeakable, and even speaking of it is impossible. Therefore, there was no need for the plucking of the flower or the smile.
Kāśyapa, how could the wisdom of one who merely stands leaning upon a position possibly reach a silent resonance with that which is difficult to express,
and truly enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality?
Linzi said: "Does form not belong to existence? Does emptiness not belong to non-existence?
Therefore, pointing to that which has form, one speaks of it, saying, 'This is form. Yet can form truly be spoken of as something to be grasped?
Pointing to that which has no form, one speaks of it, saying, 'This is emptiness. Yet can emptiness truly be spoken of as something to be grasped? Such is the profoundly deep Dharma."
Regarding that which is a realm yet not reached by either form or emptiness: does it possess form? Can it be treated as form?
Does it possess emptiness? Can it be treated as empty? It is precisely because it cannot be treated as either form or emptiness.
Therefore, one cannot grasp it as being either existent or non-existent. There is no form, no emptiness, no existence, and no non-existence.

This is why even discourse upon it is unattainable. Reaching this profoundly deep *dharmadhātu*, there is nothing by which to clarify the subtlety of non-arising (*anutpāda*), yet it arises from the wondrousness of non-birth. Who is able to know this? Who is able to know this?
Weng Sheng said, "Master, you often say that where form and emptiness do not reach is what is called the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.
May I ask how one truly enters this Dharma-gate of Non-duality? Linzi replied, "In the past, during the assembly at Vimalakīrti’s house, Mañjuśrī said:
'Regarding all dharmas, I have no speech and no discourse; I have no indication and no cognition; I am free from all questioning.'"
[The Buddha] replied, "This is the bodhisattva’s entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī again questioned Vimalakīrti, but Vimalakīrti remained silent.
Mañjuśrī praised him, saying, "To be without even speech or written characters—this is the bodhisattva’s true entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
Wengsheng was startled and marveled at this. Linzi said, "There is no need to marvel at it; however, this is not merely a matter of the Śākya [teachings]."

The Master [Vimalakīrti] was indeed so. This also occurred within the school of Confucius; thus, that which was transmitted did not reside in words, yet the transmitter did not realize how he was transmitting it.
And the receiver did not consider it obscure, yet he did not realize how he was receiving it.
If one regards Vimalakīrti’s silence as something extraordinary, then one would likewise regard the silence of Confucius as such.
"Concealment—should this not also be considered extraordinary? Yet, can the true mind and the actual ground ever be expressed in words?
Linzi said, "If it could be expressed in words, then it could also be concealed. How could one then say that 'everyone is fully endowed with it' and that 'everything is already perfected'?"
My disciple asked, "Master, you have often said that the true ground of the real mind is what is called the stage of the Tathāgata.

Is this so? Master Linzi replied, "It is. "However," the disciple continued, "is one who transcends all at once and enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata not what is called the Sudden Teaching?
Master Linzi replied, "It is. The disciple asked, "By what means can one enter the Sudden [Teaching]? Master Linzi replied, "It is through its precursor..."

Is it through seeing the nature? In the past, once the Sixth Patriarch had awakened to his original nature, the Fifth Patriarch immediately transmitted it to him as the teaching of sudden enlightenment;
this is precisely what that refers to. He asked again: "Master, you have previously said that 'seeing the nature' is the nature seeing, and 'knowing the nature' is the nature knowing.
This is subtle indeed! I pray that Master will explain this clearly to me. Linzi replied: "Since it is said that it cannot be attained..."
Yet it is seen; it cannot be known through ordinary cognition. If one neither sees nor knows, how could it be spoken of?
How then shall I speak to you? Nevertheless, within this state of non-seeing, there exists a true seeing that is not obscure;
within this state of non-knowing, there exists a true knowing that is not obscure. Therefore it is said:
"Nature is realized through self-awakening; what else could I possibly say to you? The *Platform Sutra* states:
"If every thought-moment is practiced accordingly, this is called true nature. One who awakens to this Dharma is practicing the Prajñā Dharma;
one who cultivates this practice is performing the Prajñā practice. It further states: "Using one's own True Suchness-nature, observe with wisdom..."
"All dharmas are neither grasped nor rejected; this is precisely seeing one's nature and attaining the Buddha-way. He further said:
"If you simply constantly give rise to right view within your own mind, afflictions and worldly toil can never defile it; this is seeing one's nature. He also said:
"Thus you know that all phenomena are entirely within your own mind. Why not suddenly see the true nature of Suchness from within your own mind? He further said:

If you do not awaken on your own, you must seek out a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who understands the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*), so that they may directly point out the correct path.

What are called practice, cultivation, the Dharma, the contemplation of wisdom, and the constant arising of right view—all these are intended to teach people how to see their nature and attain Buddhahood.
This is true unless one possesses a great spiritual friend who understands the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle.
Who, then, can show people the correct path so that they may see their nature and become Buddhas?
The *Platform Sūtra* says: "This matter must arise from within one's own nature.

At all times, in every thought-moment, one must purify one’s own mind, cultivate one’s own practice, see one’s own Dharma-body, see the Buddha within one’s own mind, and only then achieve self-deliverance and self-restraint."
Now, that which is called "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) is what I refer to as the true mind in its actual state—the realm where neither form nor emptiness reaches.
Does it possess defilement? Does it possess purity? As for the phrase "purifying one's own mind," how could the mind be something defiled that requires purification?
Since the mind is already free of any defilement to be purified, what need is there for cultivation, practice, or deliverance?
Regarding the precepts: generally speaking, when one speaks of "self," it carries the meaning of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).

This refers precisely to what are called the precepts of intrinsic nature, the concentration of intrinsic nature, and the wisdom of intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is said that they must arise from within intrinsic nature;

this is the fundamental principle of the Supreme Vehicle (*Ekayāna*). The Sixth Patriarch further said: "The Buddha is manifested within one's own nature; do not seek him outside the body. Furthermore—
He said: "Precisely this non-defilement is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind.
Therefore, if one wishes to see one's nature but does not arise from within one's own nature, how could such a person be able to see their own Dharma-body or the Buddha of their own mind?"
Mr. Huang asked, "Why is it called 'self'? Does it not mean the meaning of 'intrinsic nature' (svabhāva)?

Master Lin said, "Intrinsic nature is inherently pure; intrinsic nature is inherently cultivated; intrinsic nature is inherently practiced; intrinsic nature is inherently liberated; intrinsic nature is inherently precepted.
Now, since nature is fundamentally pure, it does not depend on further purification. Yet, that worldly people insist upon purifying it—is this not what is meant by 'defilement'?"

It is not so; on the contrary, do they not give rise to pure delusions? Yet, when one cultivates, practices, delivers others, and observes the precepts, all of these likewise arise from within self-nature.
If one seeks them necessarily outside of the body, one is deluded.
The Second Patriarch, Huike, came to pay his respects to the First Patriarch Bodhidharma and said, "My mind is not at peace;

I beg the Master to grant it peace. The First Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will grant you peace. The Second Patriarch sought his mind but found it utterly unobtainable. The First Patriarch said, "I have finished granting you peace.
Master Lin said: "The mind is fundamentally no-mind; how could there be such a thing as 'not being at peace'? Yet he says, 'I grant you peace.'"
The completion of "settling the mind" (anshin) is precisely the means by which one restores the fundamental substance of the mindless state.
Nevertheless, one must also understand the Sixth Patriarch’s principle of "loosening the bonds according to the circumstances."
The First Patriarch, Bodhidharma, resided at Shaolin Monastery for nine years, preaching the Dharma for the Second Patriarch, Huike.
He taught only that one should externally cease all conditions and internally remain free from the panting of the mind, making the mind like a blank wall; thus one may enter the Way.

Although Huike spoke variously about the nature of the mind, he never once grasped the principle. The First Patriarch merely refuted his errors and did not explain the essence of the non-conceptual mind to him. Hui—
Huike said, "I have already stilled all conditions. The First Patriarch asked, "Have you not fallen into annihilation? Huike replied, "It is not annihilation.
The First Patriarch said, "This is the essence of mind transmitted by all Buddhas; do not harbor further doubt.
That which is called the essence of mind without thought is not what I mean by 'a place where form and emptiness do not reach. It is the manifestation of all things."
It is accomplished. Now, as for "resting," it is resting; it is resting without anything upon which to rest.
If one were to rest with something upon which to rest, would this not give rise to the delusion of the mind and result in annihilationism?

To say that "the mind is like a wall" is precisely for the purpose of externally ceasing all conditions, resting in a state where there is nothing upon which to rest. Therefore, it is said that this can be done.
Entering the Way, the Third Patriarch Sengcan said: "If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not loathe the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
If you do not loathe the six sense-objects, you are identical to perfect enlightenment. Yet, within the true ground of the other shore, the six sense-objects fundamentally do not exist.

To speak of 'loathing the six sense-objects' is simply the mind itself; does this not act as an adversary to the external six sense-objects? This would then belong to the category of remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*)."—The Fourth Patriarch.
Daoxin said: "Objective conditions have neither good nor bad; good and bad arise from the mind.

Since the mind is fundamentally sovereign, if one necessarily gives rise to thoughts to confront the six sense objects, would this not be called losing its fundamental essence of sovereignty? He further said:

"Whenever the eyes encounter objects or the senses meet with conditions, these are all the wondrous functioning of the Buddha. Regarding the phrase "whenever the eyes encounter objects," it is because conditions themselves do not exist [independently].
I am also thus; with the mind attaining mastery, wondrous function manifests before one. The Sixth Patriarch Huineng said: "The Buddha-dharma is in the world;
it is not separate from worldly awakening. To leave the world to seek Bodhi is like seeking a hare's horn. If you loathe the six sense-objects, you will give rise to a distaste for the world.
To feel distaste for and leave the world is not called wisdom; how then could you see your nature and enter the Sudden Teaching? Thus he spoke of non-existence.
This is indeed the realization of supreme, perfect enlightenment!

The Third Patriarch Sengcan said: "To dispel existence by means of non-existence, and to turn one's back on emptiness from within emptiness. As for what he meant by "turning one's back on emptiness from within emptiness":
Is this not the emptiness of the so-called "characteristic of emptiness"? That which is called the "emptiness of turning away from emptiness"—is this not the "emptiness within emptiness"?

It is further said: "To return to the root is to attain the essential meaning; to follow after illumination is to lose the source. If one reflects back for even a moment, it surpasses the former emptiness.
Now, what is called the "root" and the "source" is my original nature—the emptiness within emptiness. And as for what is called "reflecting back":

This is the reflection back upon the emptiness within emptiness. Now that one knows this reflection back upon the emptiness within emptiness, how could it not be superior to the previous emptiness that still possesses the mark of emptiness?

As for those who follow the gate of emptiness, should they not understand how to enter the gate through such reflection, rather than falsely attempting to turn their backs on emptiness by departing from it?

Hesheng asked, "Third Patriarch, is there a difference between the 'illumination' of *fanzhao* (reflective illumination) and the 'illumination' of 'illuminating and seeing' (*zhàojiàn*) in the *Heart Sūtra*?
Linzi said, "The illumination of *fanzhao* is the 'contemplation' (*guān*) of Avalokiteśvara.

Therefore, as for 'illuminating and seeing,' it refers to having already reached the other shore and then illuminating and seeing that within this other shore, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty. This is *fanzhao*."
This is because, having not yet reached the other shore, one instead turns inward to observe and illuminate within, desiring thereby to see one's nature.

The *Platform Sutra* says: "Depart from delusion and depart from awakening, and constantly give rise to *prajñā*; eliminate the true and eliminate the false, and you will immediately see the Buddha-nature.
From this, I have come to know that departing from delusion to reach awakening—awakening is itself delusion; eliminating the false to reach the true—the true is itself the false.
Therefore, awakening and delusion are not two; truth and falsehood are equal. This is what those who wish to see their nature must understand.

Long ago, when a non-Buddhist asked the World-Honored One, "I do not ask for words regarding existence, nor do I ask for words regarding non-existence," the World-Honored One remained silent for a long time.
The non-Buddhist then praised him, saying, "The World-Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, has cleared away the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to enter."
He then paid his respects and departed. The World-Honored One said of him, "A fine horse moves when it sees the shadow of the whip.
As for the World-Honored One’s long silence, is this not what the Sixth Patriarch called "not thinking of good, not thinking of evil"—the face of original nature?
This is precisely what I mean by "the place where the emptiness of form does not reach. Therefore, those who understand this are called "within the gate";
those who are deluded regarding it are called "outsiders" (tīrthikas).
Linzi said: "What I call the 'ground of reality' is what the Buddhists call the 'mind that illumines.
The mind is the ground. What I call the 'true mind' is what the Buddhists call the 'nature that realizes.
Nature is the sovereign. If one cannot illumine the ground of the mind, how could one possibly realize the nature?"
"Is it the King? Indeed, the nature of the mind is one and the same. However, wherever the true mind resides, that very place is designated as 'mind.
Thus it is said that the mind is the earth. Confucius said, 'He who abides in benevolence with his whole heart,' and here too the mind is spoken of in terms of the earth.
His phrase 'with his whole heart' (zhōngxīn) refers to what is called the center; the center is the earth. I have previously examined the scriptures of these two traditions.
I have appended my humble views to this; therefore, I shall address them by means of the mind and its nature (*xing*). That which has not yet sprouted from the mind is called nature;
that which has already sprouted from nature is called the mind. If one speaks of nature alone, there is the nature conferred by Heaven (*tian-ming zhi xing*).
There is the nature of qi and temperament. Furthermore, speaking specifically of the mind, there is the mind of the five elements and the mind of the Center.
Mr. Ruan asked: "Master, you once said that between the mind and heaven and earth, which is greater? You replied, 'The mind is greater.

Yet in the *Xingjiao* (Discourse on Nature and Mind), it says 'carrying [heaven and earth] within the mind. What kind of mind is this? Linzi said: "This is what is called being without fixed location and without..."
Regarding the true mind of the essence: this true mind is the nature, the true nature; it is the mind that pervades the realm of empty space, such that there is nothing it does not encompass.
Now, does this empty space have boundaries? Or is it without boundaries? Can it be demarcated by boundaries?
Or can it not be demarcated by boundaries? One who has personally reached the other shore should [consider this].
Know this for yourself. Thus, those who perceive their nature see only this; those who enter the Sudden Teaching enter only this.
*General Discussion of the Heart Sūtra* (End).
Written by my own hand at the conclusion of the *General Discussion of the Heart Sūtra*.
Now, as for what is called a "General Discourse" (*gai-ron*), it is because the primary meaning of the *Heart Sūtra* cannot be expressed through names or words;

thus, one discusses it by way of a general overview. When I first composed this General Discourse to show it to the virtuous friends of the school of nature (*shōmon*), they were greatly pleased and requested that I divide it into chapters and provide an explanation. I have long considered that, from the Sixth Patriarch downward, the Buddha-dharma...
It is not understood that what is called the Supreme Vehicle (Ekayāna) is, in fact, a great public case (kōan) already manifest before us.
Consequently, there are many who mistake the emptiness of suffering for a stubborn, nihilistic void;
they avoid sensory dust and sit in withered stillness, taking mere annihilation to be nirvana. Thus, the ultimate teaching of Śākyamuni fails to illuminate the world.
That this work has been constantly criticized by the Confucian scholars makes me privately grieve for them;
therefore, I have again composed a brief commentary on the Heart Sūtra and this general treatise as two separate volumes. I am now old, and my physical vigor no longer suffices.
In these two books, how could one say there are redundant phrases or a loss of sequential order? Not only was there no leisure for collation, but it was also impossible to collate them.
This was the work of the Master of the Three Teachings, Longjiang Zhao’en.
